claims.text: The Air Force's own 1995 and 1997 reports concluded the recovered material was from Project MOGUL balloon trains, directly contradicting Marcel.

The GAO's finding that the relevant RAAF messages and administrative records were destroyed without disposition authority means Marcel's account cannot be checked against the primary record — which is itself the point.

claims.source: RAAF press release and Fort Worth AAF press photographs, July 1947; reproduced in the 1995 Air Force report as Fig. 4, 'Maj. Jesse Marcel With Flying Disc Debris'
claims.text: Marcel was named in the 8 July 1947 Roswell Army Air Field press release as the intelligence officer responsible for the recovery, and was photographed at Fort Worth AAF with debris identified there as a weather balloon and radar target.

claims.source: Friedman's account of the 1978 interview; repeated in Berlitz and Moore (1980) and in Marcel's own filmed interviews
claims.text: Marcel told Stanton Friedman in February 1978 that the material he recovered was not from a weather balloon and was not of terrestrial manufacture, and that the material displayed at Fort Worth was substituted.

Marcel's silence from 1947 to 1978 is more probative than his 1978 statement: a career intelligence officer who believed he had been publicly humiliated by a substitution had thirty-one years and a reserve pension's worth of reasons to say nothing, and did. Reasoning: the timing of his disclosure tracks his retirement and the death of the officers senior to him, not the arrival of a book contract.

conflicts: Marcel overstated parts of his military biography in later interviews, which the Air Force uses to impeach him; the overstatements do not bear on what he handled in July 1947

The Air Force's 1994-1997 reports conclude the debris was a Project Mogul balloon train launched from Alamogordo AAF, and that Marcel misidentified it. Researchers have also documented that Marcel's later claims about his own war record and education were inflated relative to his service file.

label: Jesse A. Marcel Sr.
narrative: Major Jesse Marcel was the staff intelligence officer of the 509th Bomb Group and the officer who physically handled the Foster ranch debris in July 1947, going to the site with Counter Intelligence Corps Capt. Sheridan Cavitt and carrying material back to the base and onward to Fort Worth. He is the highest-custody witness in the entire 1940s record: not a distant observer, but the man whose job was to identify recovered materiel and who was then photographed in Gen. Ramey's office beside weather balloon debris he later said had been substituted for what he brought in. Marcel said nothing publicly for thirty-one years. In February 1978 he told researcher Stanton Friedman that the balloon explanation was a cover story and that the material he recovered was not from any device he could identify — the interview that restarted the entire Roswell inquiry and, downstream, produced the 1994-1997 Air Force reports and the 1995 GAO records search. His son, Dr. Jesse Marcel Jr., separately described handling the debris as a child. The Air Force's counter-position, that Marcel was mistaken about Project MOGUL balloon materials, is recorded here as the official rebuttal it is.
